title: Fragile Links
statement: A data center has hubs numbered 0 to hubs - 1 joined by two-way cables in links (at most one cable per pair, never a hub to itself). A cable is fragile if cutting it alone would split some pair of hubs that can currently reach each other. Return every fragile cable as [smaller hub, larger hub], sorted by the first hub and then the second.
constraints: 0 <= a, b < hubs, a != b, and each pair appears at most once

examples.explanation: The triangle 0-1-2 survives any single cut, but cutting [1, 3] isolates hub 3.

hints.content: Cutting a cable and checking connectivity for each cable works, but repeats a full traversal per cable.
A cable is fragile exactly when it is not part of any cycle.
Run a depth-first search and number hubs in visiting order. For each hub compute low: the earliest visiting number reachable from its subtree using at most one non-tree cable.
A tree cable from parent p to child c is fragile exactly when low[c] > order[p]: nothing below c reaches back to p or above.
Skip only the cable you arrived by (track it by index), take the minimum with children's low values after they finish, and sort the results at the end.

testCases.explanation: The triangle 0-1-2 survives any single cut, but cutting [1, 3] isolates hub 3.
A lone hub has no cables.
Every cable in a chain is fragile.
A ring has no fragile cables.
Two triangles joined by [2, 3], plus a tail [5, 6].
Separate clusters: every cable is fragile, reported in sorted order.

solutions.title: Remove each cable and recount clusters
solutions.intuition: A cable is fragile if removing it increases the number of connected clusters.
solutions.approach: Count clusters with union-find using all cables. For each cable, recount without it and keep the cable if the count went up. Normalize and sort.
solutions.pseudocode:
base = clusters(all); for e: if clusters(all except e) > base: keep e
return sorted normalized kept
commonMistakes: Checking only whether the two endpoints are still connected but comparing the wrong way round.
Returning cables in input order or with unnormalized endpoints.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Removing each cable and recounting clusters follows the definition directly. It costs a full union-find pass per cable, roughly quadratic.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: Removing [0,1], [1,2] or [2,0] leaves the triangle connected through the other two.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Removing [1,3] isolates hub 3, so only [1,3] is fragile.

solutions.title: Tarjan's bridge-finding DFS
solutions.intuition: A tree cable is a bridge when the child's subtree has no back cable reaching the parent or above, which the low values capture.
solutions.approach: DFS from every unvisited hub, assigning order and low. For each neighbor other than via the arrival cable: if unvisited, recurse, then low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]) and report the cable if low[v] > order[u]; if visited, low[u] = min(low[u], order[v]). Sort the bridges.
solutions.timeComplexity: O(n + m) plus sorting the bridges
commonMistakes: Skipping the parent hub instead of the arrival cable; with parallel cables that would be wrong (they are excluded here, but tracking the cable index is the robust habit).
Using low[v] >= order[u], which is the articulation-point test, not the bridge test.
solutions.interviewExplanation: A cable is a bridge iff it lies on no cycle. In a DFS tree every non-tree cable closes a cycle, so I compute low[u], the earliest discovery time reachable from u's subtree with one back cable. A tree cable (u, v) is a bridge exactly when low[v] > order[u]. One DFS gives O(n + m). For very deep graphs I'd make the DFS iterative to avoid stack limits.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: DFS 0 → 1 → 2. The back cable 2–0 gives low[2] = 0, which flows up: low[1] = 0.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: From 1, visit 3: low[3] = order[3] = 3 > order[1] = 1, so [1,3] is a bridge.

steps.title: Step 3
steps.content: low[2] = 0 is not greater than order[1], and low[1] = 0 is not greater than order[0], so those cables are not bridges.
